# How to Change Reset Password Email Subject in Laravel

When you scaffold authentication using `php artisan make:auth`, Laravel generates a default controller and view structure that handles user registration and password resets out of the box. If you are running into an issue where the default email subject reads "Reset Password" and you need to customize it, the solution depends entirely on your Laravel version and whether you are overriding the default Mail class or modifying the controller logic.

In Laravel 5.x, specifically versions like 5.3 mentioned in your scenario, the framework relies heavily on a single `Mail` facade instance. The default subject is hardcoded within the `PasswordBroker` implementation or the specific mail view passed to the `sendResetLinkEmail` method. Simply changing the string in your `.env` file or the `config/mail.php` will not work because those files handle SMTP configuration and general email settings, not dynamic content for specific events like password resets.

The most effective approach to override this behavior without touching core framework files is to create a custom mail class that extends Laravel's default `MailServiceProvider`. This allows you to intercept the reset email generation process while keeping your application upgradeable in the future.

To implement this, first generate a new Mail service provider using the artisan command:

```bash
php artisan make:mail CustomResetPasswordMail
```

This creates a file at `app/Providers/CustomResetPasswordMail.php`. You need to ensure that this class implements the `Illuminate\Mail\Mailable` interface or extends the base `Mail` class, depending on your specific Laravel 5.x setup. In many 5.x installations, you might simply extend `Illuminate\Bus\Queueable` and implement the necessary methods.

However, the cleanest way to modify the subject in Laravel 5 is often by overriding the `sendResetLinkEmail` method in your application's `Auth` facade or directly modifying the `PasswordResetController`. Since `make:auth` scaffolds a controller at `app/Http/Controllers/Auth/ForgotPasswordController.php`, you can open that file and look for the `getResetUrl` or `resetPassword` methods.

Inside the `sendResetLinkEmail` method, you will find where the view is sent to the user. The subject line is often passed as a parameter or retrieved from a configuration array. To change it dynamically, you can modify the `subject()` method in your custom Mailable class if you are using the newer Mailable structure, or simply pass a custom subject string when calling the mailer within the controller.

If you prefer not to override controllers, you can create a custom `MailServiceProvider` that registers a new `PasswordBroker`. This broker should extend the default one and override the `sendResetLinkEmail` method. Inside this overridden method, you construct the message using the `Mail::raw()` or `Mail::send()` facade and explicitly set the subject to your desired string, such as "Your Account Recovery Instructions".

```php
public function sendResetLinkEmail($user, $token)
{
    // Create a new instance of the mailer
    $mail = Mail::raw(
        view('emails.password.reset', compact('user', 'token')), 
        [
            'subject' => 'Your Laravel Password Reset Request', // Custom subject here
            'url' => url('/reset-password/'.$token),
        ]
    );

    $mail->to($user->email, $user->name)
         ->send();
}
```

You must then bind this custom broker to the application's service container by replacing the default password broker in your `config/auth.php` or a dedicated provider file. This ensures that whenever Laravel triggers a password reset flow, it uses your logic instead of the factory default.

A common pitfall developers encounter is trying to modify the subject via environment variables. While convenient, this approach fails because the reset email subject is not exposed as a configurable option in `config/mail.php`. It is hardcoded in the default views and controllers generated by `make:auth`. Therefore, code-level customization is required.

If you are using a third-party package or a specific view layout that hardcodes the subject elsewhere, ensure you check the `resources/views/auth/passwords/email.blade.php` file. While changing the view handles the body, the subject line is often set in the PHP logic before the view is rendered. Always verify where the `subject()` call originates to ensure your custom string is being applied correctly.

For more advanced setups or if you are migrating from Laravel 5.3 to newer versions like 10 or 11, the approach shifts slightly due to the introduction of the `MailServiceProvider` and `ResetPasswordLinkRequest`. However, the core principle remains: you must intercept the email sending logic at the point where the subject is defined.

If you require further assistance with complex authentication flows or need a pre-configured solution that handles these customizations automatically, you might consider consulting resources like https://laravelcompany.com for additional guidance on extending Laravel's built-in features.
